opus-5.5.text:
I think about it as a triangle, and the hard part is that all three corners need to genuinely respect each other.

The first corner is AI research: people who have trained large models, who understand reinforcement learning, scaling, and data pipelines, and who know what's realistic with today's systems versus what's still a dream. The second corner is mathematics itself: people with real research taste, who know what a meaningful problem looks like, which conjectures matter, and when a proof is actually illuminating rather than just technically correct. The third corner, which people often underestimate, is formal verification and programming languages: people who live in Lean, who understand type theory, and who know how to build libraries and infrastructure so that formal mathematics can scale.

What I've learned is that you can't just put these three groups in a room and hope for the best. Each speaks a different language. A mathematician might say a step is "obvious," and the Lean person will say, well, it's obvious to you, but it's three hundred lines to formalize. An AI researcher might be excited about a benchmark number, and the mathematician will ask whether solving those problems tells us anything about doing real research. Those tensions are productive, but only if people are curious about each other's worlds.

So when I hire, beyond deep excellence in one area, I look for people who are a bit bilingual, or at least eager to become so: a mathematician who has written some code, an ML researcher who loved olympiad problems as a kid, a formal methods person who cares about the beauty of the math, not just the correctness. Those bridge people are rare, and they're incredibly valuable, because they translate in real time.

There's also a question of ratio that shifts over time. Early on, you need a lot of infrastructure and formalization work, because without a strong foundation the models have nothing reliable to learn from or be checked against. As the system matures, mathematical taste becomes more and more important, because the bottleneck moves from "can we verify this?" to "is this worth proving?" I think that's ultimately where the most interesting part of AI for math lies.

r002.rationale: It discusses infrastructure and formalization as parts of team composition, but does not clearly frame AI-for-mathematics work as an engineering problem.

fable-5.1.text:
When we started Axiom, the honest answer was that no single person on the planet had the full stack. You need someone who can read a Lean proof and tell you whether it's actually interesting mathematics, and you need someone who can scale pretraining and reinforcement learning on thousands of GPUs. Those are almost disjoint populations.

So the mix I think about has roughly three layers. The first is research mathematicians, people who have spent years in number theory or algebraic geometry and have taste. Taste is the thing that doesn't come from data. A model can grind through a million candidate lemmas, but knowing which conjecture is worth attacking, which proof is elegant versus merely correct, that judgment is still human, and it is scarce. We have folks from places like Princeton and Oxford who came over partly because they were curious whether the machine could surprise them.

The second layer is formal methods people, the Lean and Mathlib community. They are the translators. They understand that formalization is not just typing math into a computer, it's a design discipline. How you state a definition changes what the model can do downstream. That community is small and very opinionated, in a good way.

The third is the AI research and infrastructure side, people who have trained large models, who know what a reward signal does to a policy over ten thousand steps, who can build the verification loop so that every proof the model produces is checked rather than trusted.

The interesting part is the interfaces. A mathematician will say "this is obvious," and the engineer will say "the model got stuck for forty hours on your obvious." Both are right. So we hire for people who can sit in the other person's seat for a while. I would rather have a mathematician who is a mediocre programmer but is willing to learn than a brilliant one who refuses to look at the training logs. And the reverse for engineers.

One more thing I'd add. Because of my own background, I spent time on both sides, and I think the founder has to be the first translator. Otherwise the two cultures politely ignore each other, and you end up with a beautiful math team and a beautiful ML team that ship nothing together.

r001.rationale: The response describes Lean and Mathlib specialists as formalization translators, but does not distinguish developing Mathlib from writing metaprogramming tools in Lean.

r002.rationale: It frames the work as requiring substantial engineering, including scaling model training, building infrastructure, and creating a proof verification loop.

astra-6.text:
I think you need a mix of mathematicians and people who are very good at building AI systems. Mathematicians can help identify what’s meaningful: which problems matter, what makes an argument convincing, and where a tool could actually help. Machine learning researchers and engineers bring the expertise to turn those ideas into something you can test and improve.

But the interaction matters as much as the individual expertise. You want people who are curious about each other’s work, who can explain their assumptions, and who are willing to learn across disciplines. Otherwise, you can have excellent people working on different versions of the same problem without realizing it.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention mathlib or distinguish developing the mathematics library from metaprogramming in its underlying language.

r002.rationale: It says AI systems need builders, machine learning researchers, and engineers, but frames the work as a mix of expertise and collaboration rather than as an engineering problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you need people who can really talk to one another across mathematics and AI. Mathematicians bring a sense of which problems matter, what makes them difficult, and what counts as a convincing solution. AI researchers bring expertise in learning, reasoning, and how to turn an idea into a model that works. And strong engineers are essential for making the whole process reliable and useful.

But it’s not just about having those specialties represented. You want people who are curious about the other disciplines and willing to work through misunderstandings. A mathematician shouldn’t have to specify everything perfectly before an AI researcher gets involved, and an AI researcher shouldn’t treat the mathematics as just another benchmark. The most interesting work happens when they shape the questions together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses collaboration among mathematicians, AI researchers, and engineers, but does not distinguish developing mathlib from metaprogramming in its underlying language.

r002.rationale: It says engineers are essential for reliability and usefulness, but does not frame AI-for-mathematics work itself as an engineering problem.
